a: Put the ram's horn to your mouth!
t: The horn: an alarm, not music
p: The shofar was blown to warn of an enemy. Hosea has already blown it once, at Gibeah (5:8).
b: The Hebrew shofar is a ram's horn, the sentry's alarm: when an enemy comes, the watchman blows it and the people must act (Jeremiah 6:17; Ezekiel 33:2-6). The verse gives no speaker and no one to blow it. Most readers hear the LORD ordering the prophet to sound the alarm, as at 5:8 ("Blow the ram's horn in Gibeah"). The word translated "mouth" is literally the palate, the roof of the mouth, where a trumpeter's breath begins. The command at the head of chapter 8 sets the tone: the rest of the chapter is an alarm, not a lesson. Compare the prophet as "watchman" at 9:8.

a: Like an eagle, he swoops on
p: Nearly everyone reads the eagle as an enemy, most often Assyria. The Hebrew has no verb and no name.
b: The Hebrew has only "like the eagle over the house of the LORD". The Plain supplies "he swoops" because English needs a verb. The nesher is the griffon vulture as well as the eagle, a bird that circles over a body. Views: (1) Assyria, the commonest reading, matching the later pictures of an army as a bird of prey (Deuteronomy 28:49; Jeremiah 48:40; Habakkuk 1:8); (2) an unnamed enemy, left open so that the hearer fills in the name; (3) the LORD himself, who is compared to an eagle at Deuteronomy 32:11 but is never called a vulture; few take it so. The Greek begins differently ("Into their bosom like the earth, like an eagle against the house of the LORD"), reading the first words of the verse another way.

p: The 'house of the LORD' may be the Temple at Jerusalem, a shrine in the north, the land, or the people.
b: Four readings are held. (1) A shrine: the sanctuary at Bethel or Samaria, the "house" the northern kingdom actually had. (2) The Jerusalem Temple, which would put Judah under the eagle's shadow (the chapter ends with Judah, 8:14). (3) The land, which the LORD calls "my house" in 9:15 ("I will drive them out of my house"). (4) The people, the LORD's household (compare Numbers 12:7, "my whole house"). In 9:15 the context is exile from the land, which makes (3) and (4) the likeliest in Hosea's own usage; (1) fits the calf and altars of the rest of the chapter. A reader does not have to choose: the shrine, the land and the people were one thing to a hearer in Samaria.

p: Torah means 'teaching' and 'law'. Hosea uses it for both the priests' instruction and a written body of law.
b: Torah is "teaching" in the Plain wherever a parent, priest or prophet instructs (4:6, "the teaching of your God") and "law" where a written code seems meant. Here it stands beside "covenant", and in 8:12 the LORD says he "wrote" it out, so "law" is the better English. Some scholars hear in 8:1 the language of Deuteronomy (the covenant broken, the law not kept); others think Hosea has the priests' oral teaching in mind in both verses. Whether Hosea knew a written law book is debated; the verse uses the word in the sense of the LORD's whole expressed will for Israel. See 8:12.

t: "We know you": the cry that is not enough
p: The people claim the very thing the LORD says they lack.
b: The words are the people's confession in a crisis: "My God, we know you." The charge in this book is that there is "no knowledge of God" in the land (4:1) and that the people were "destroyed because they have no knowledge" (4:6). To know God (yada') means to be committed to him in covenant, to acknowledge him by loyalty and by justice, not only to say his name. The next verse says what their words do not cover: "Israel has cast off the good." The same cry in a crisis marks 6:1-3 and 7:14, in which the people turn to the LORD only when hurt. At 13:4 the LORD says the same thing from his side: "You are to know no god but me."

t: 'The good': a thing, a person, or God?
p: 'The good' may be the covenant way, the law, or God himself.
b: The Hebrew tov has no further word with it. Readers take it as (1) what is good, the right way of life the LORD asked for (Micah 6:8: "Human being, he has told you what is good"), (2) the good gifts of the covenant, the land and its blessings (Deuteronomy 26:11), or (3) God as the good one, since "good" is a name for him in Psalm 34:8 and Psalm 73:1. The Plain keeps "the good" so that all three stay open. The verb zanach, "cast off", is the same one used of the LORD's rejection of the calf in 8:5, so the people reject the LORD's good and the LORD rejects their calf.
orig: זָנַח טוֹב (zanach tov), 'cast off the good'

a: They crowned kings, but the choice was not mine.
p: After Jeroboam II, four of the next six kings of Israel took the throne by killing the king before them.
b: Jeroboam II died about 753 BC after a reign of over forty years. His successors were: Zechariah (six months, killed), Shallum (a month, killed), Menahem (ten years), Pekahiah (killed), Pekah (killed) and Hoshea, the last. The pattern is told in the Plain's Kings: "Shallum son of Jabesh plotted against him. He struck him down in front of the people and killed him, and he reigned in his place." (2 Kings 15:10). Menahem did the same to Shallum (2 Kings 15:14), Pekah to Pekahiah (2 Kings 15:25) and Hoshea to Pekah (2 Kings 15:30). Hosea's own words about this fever are in 7:3-7 and 13:10-11. The LORD had named some northern kings through prophets (1 Kings 11:29-39; 2 Kings 9:1-13), so Hosea is not saying every northern throne was illegitimate. He is saying that these were taken, not given.
r: 2 Kings 15:10; 2 Kings 15:14; 2 Kings 15:25; 2 Kings 15:30; Hosea 7:3-7; Hosea 13:10-11; 1 Kings 11:29-39

p: Hosea is the only writer who ties a calf to Samaria. Jeroboam's two calves stood at Bethel and Dan.
b: When Jeroboam I split off the northern kingdom he made two golden calves and put them at Bethel and Dan: "So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold." (1 Kings 12:28), and "He placed one calf in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan." (1 Kings 12:29). Samaria is not named in the story, so "the calf of Samaria" (8:6) has been read in three ways: Bethel's calf, called by the capital's name because the capital stood for the kingdom; a separate image in Samaria itself; or a loose name for the whole calf-cult. The verse in 10:5 speaks of "the heifers of Beth-aven", and 13:2 of men who "kiss calves". The Hebrew 'egel is a young bull. Many scholars take such images as a pedestal for the LORD (as the cherubim were), not a second god; Hosea does not allow that defense in 8:6.
r: 1 Kings 12:28; 1 Kings 12:29; Exodus 32:4; 2 Kings 10:29; Hosea 10:5; Hosea 13:2

p: The Hebrew word occurs only here. It is read as 'splinters' or 'fragments'; some link it with Aramaic 'flames'.
b: The Hebrew shevavim is found nowhere else in the Bible. The commonest guess is "splinters" or "chips", the pieces of a wooden core with a thin metal coat once it is broken up. A second guess links it with the Aramaic shevivin of Daniel 7:9 ("flames"), so that the calf would go up in fire. The Greek has "a deceiver" (planon), the calf as a thing that leads astray. All agree on the sense: the calf will not last.

p: The saying 'sow the wind, reap the whirlwind' comes from here. The Plain keeps the two Hebrew words apart.
b: The Hebrew has ruach, "wind", for the seed and suphah, "storm wind", for the harvest. Wind is a Hosea word for emptiness: Ephraim "herds the wind" and "runs after the scorching east wind" (12:1), and 13:3 compares the people to chaff blown off a threshing floor. The point is the same as in the rest of the verse: what is sown is worth nothing and what is reaped is ruin (10:13). The English proverb has its own life; the Plain does not use its wording because the Hebrew does not say "the" wind or "the" whirlwind. The nearest saying elsewhere is Job 4:8.
orig: רוּחַ יִזְרָעוּ וְסוּפָתָה יִקְצֹרוּ (ruach yizra'u ve-suphatah yiqtsoru)

a: like a jar that no one wants
p: Jeremiah uses the same picture for a rejected king.
b: The Hebrew is "a vessel in which there is no pleasure". A pot no one wants is thrown out and smashed. Jeremiah uses almost the same line for the king Jehoiachin: "Is he a vessel no one delights in?" (Jeremiah 22:28), and the potter's smashed jar of Jeremiah 19 follows the same thought. Paul uses the potter's vessels in another way (Romans 9:21-23). The line is Hosea's way of saying that being "among the nations" is not a promotion for Israel but a disposal.

p: Menahem paid tribute to Assyria. Later kings sent to Egypt as well.
b: Hosea speaks of Ephraim's foreign policy in many places (5:13; 7:8-11; 12:1). The best-known case: "Pul king of Assyria came into the land. Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, so that Pul's hands would be with him and would make the kingdom firm in Menahem's hand." (2 Kings 15:19). "Pul" is generally taken as another name for Tiglath-pileser III. Hoshea later paid tribute to Shalmaneser V, and then sent to Egypt for help, which brought on the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 17:3-4). To the prophet each deal is a purchase of "lovers", the word that chapter 2 uses for Baal: Israel the wife is paying her lovers (see 2:12 and 9:1, "a prostitute's pay"). That the paying runs in the wrong direction is the bitter edge of the picture.
r: 2 Kings 15:19; 2 Kings 17:3; 2 Kings 17:4; Hosea 5:13; Hosea 7:11; Hosea 2:12

a: like a wild donkey off by itself
p: The Hebrew sounds like Ephraim: pere' and Efrayim.
b: Hosea likes to turn a name into a pun. Pere', "wild donkey", sounds like the first half of Efrayim. The wild donkey is a loner, hard to catch, stubborn and fast: the picture Genesis 16:12 gives of Ishmael ("a wild donkey of a man"), and one used of the stubborn heart in Job 39:5-8. Ephraim thinks he is free, running alone in the desert, but the donkey who wanders there is in danger. Hosea plays on Ephraim's name again in 9:16 and 13:15 ("bears fruit"). Note that "Ephraim" in this book usually means the whole northern kingdom.
orig: פֶּרֶא בּוֹדֵד לוֹ (pere' boded lo), 'a wild donkey alone to himself'

t: The title of an Assyrian king
p: 'King of princes' is a Hebrew version of the Assyrian title 'king of kings'.
b: The Assyrian emperors called themselves "king of kings" (in Akkadian sharru sharrani) and boasted that their governors were kings. Isaiah has the Assyrian king say it: "Aren't my officers kings, every one of them?" (Isaiah 10:8). Hosea's "king of princes" is the same idea with a sneer: the king over the princes (in Hebrew sarim, "officials, princes"), the king whose officials are as good as kings. The verse says that after Ephraim has paid for help the same ruler will lean on them.

p: The Hebrew verb can come from three roots. The Greek has a different line.
b: The Hebrew vayyachelu can be (1) from chul, "writhe, twist in pain", as in labor (the Plain's choice), (2) from chalal II, "begin" ("they will begin to diminish..."), or (3) from chalah, "grow weak". The Greek reads, "They will cease a little from anointing a king and rulers", which follows a different pointing and takes "burden" as "anointing". The Plain's "writhe" fits the weight in the next line: the load of the king of princes. A reader who follows (2) gets nearly the same meaning: in a little while they will begin to feel it.

p: The Hebrew 'for sin' can mean 'for sin offerings' or 'for sinning'. The verse may play on both.
b: The Hebrew lachato is an infinitive, "for sinning", but the noun chatta't also names the sin offering of Leviticus 4. So the line can say that Ephraim built altars in order to be forgiven, and that these altars became places to sin. Hosea does not choose, and the Plain keeps "for sin". The charge fits 4:8, where priests "feed on the sin" of the people; the more sin offerings are brought, the better they eat. For the people's trust in sacrifice rather than in the LORD see 6:6 and 8:13.

t: A written law in the eighth century?
p: The verse says the LORD writes (or has written) his law down for Israel. How much of the Pentateuch Hosea knew is debated.
b: The Hebrew verb katav, "write", points to a written law (Exodus 24:12; 34:27; Deuteronomy 31:9). Scholars differ on how much was written by Hosea's day. A traditional reading holds that Israel had the Torah of Moses. A critical reading finds the roots of the later Pentateuch, or of Deuteronomy, in the prophet's circle in the north, and notes that Hosea shares much language and many themes with Deuteronomy (loyal love, love of God, the Exodus, the warning against the Baals). In Hosea the "points" (rubbe) of the law are many, perhaps a hint at a long list of rulings. The verb is in the imperfect, so it can be "I write", "I would write" or "I kept writing"; the Plain reads it as "though I write". The Ketiv and the Qere have the same verb, spelled two ways; they differ in the next word. See the variant, which gives the Ketiv-Qere and the Greek.

p: The law is treated like something that belongs to outsiders.
b: The Hebrew zar means "foreign, strange", the word for a foreigner or an outsider (5:7: "strange children"). The line can say the law is treated (1) as strange, something no one recognizes, (2) as foreign, belonging to another people, or (3) as someone else's affair, a matter for experts. The effect is the same as in 4:6, where the people have forgotten the teaching of their God. The sharpest reading is that Israel thinks of the LORD's law as a foreign law, while treating foreign gods as native.

a: They offer sacrifices as gifts to me.
t: A word that occurs only once
p: The Hebrew word for 'gifts' is not found elsewhere. The verse is hard in several places.
b: The first half of the verse uses havhav (in "the sacrifices of my gifts"), a word found nowhere else in the Bible. The translation "gifts" is a guess from the sense. Others connect it to a word for "love gifts" or break the line differently ("As for the sacrifices of the gifts to me, they sacrifice meat and eat it"). The Greek has "if they sacrifice a sacrifice and eat flesh, the LORD will not accept them". The sense is clear: the sacrifice is a meal for the worshipers, and the LORD takes no pleasure in it. For the rule that a sacrifice must come from a faithful heart see 6:6; Amos 5:21-22; Isaiah 1:11-17.
orig: הַבְהָבַי (havhavay), a word found only here

a: They will go back to Egypt.
p: A threat to reverse the Exodus. Egypt may be real, or a name for slavery.
b: The closest earlier text is the curse of Deuteronomy 28:68: "The LORD will ship you back to Egypt, on the very road I told you that you would never see again." Hosea repeats it in 9:3, 6 and 11:5, where the same people who were brought out will be taken back. Two readings: (1) Egypt as a place: some of the northerners fled there (7:11, 16; 12:1), and Jeremiah 44 shows Judeans in Egypt later; (2) Egypt as a name for slavery, with Assyria as the real destination (11:5: "To the land of Egypt they will not return, but Assyria himself will be their king"). A reader who holds both can say that Hosea is using Egypt for any place where Israel is slave again.
r: Deuteronomy 28:68; Hosea 9:3; Hosea 9:6; Hosea 11:5; Hosea 12:9; Jeremiah 44:1

p: Uzziah and Jotham built forts and towers. Many critics see this line as a Judean addition.
b: Judah under Uzziah and Jotham was strong: "In Jerusalem Uzziah built towers by the Corner Gate, by the Valley Gate and by the bend in the wall, and he made them strong." (2 Chronicles 26:9), and "Towns he built in Judah's hill country, and in the wooded hills he built forts and towers." (2 Chronicles 27:4). Many critics hold that the lines about Judah in Hosea (1:7; 4:15; 5:5, 10; 6:11; 8:14; 12:2) come from Judean readers after 722 who applied the book to themselves. Others say Hosea may well have warned the south while the north fell. Amos 2:5 uses the same fire-and-fortress language against Judah.

t: Prostitution as a name for worship of other gods
p: The verb is zanah. The Plain keeps the literal word, as in 4:12 and 1:2.
b: Zanah is the ordinary Hebrew verb for acting as a prostitute. Hosea uses it for Israel's turning from the LORD to Baal and the other gods (4:12; 5:3; 9:1), with the husband-wife image of chapters 1-3 behind it. The Plain keeps the plain word, because "unfaithful" or "went astray" soften what Hosea's hearers would have heard. Whether the picture also describes real sex at the shrines is debated. Older commentaries spoke of "sacred prostitution"; many modern scholars doubt that any such office existed in Israel or Canaan and read the word as a metaphor for loyalty given to another. The notes at 4:12-14 in the first part of the book discuss it.

t: The pay of a prostitute and the gifts of Baal
p: Israel counts the harvest as a payment from Baal, as in 2:12.
b: The Hebrew etnan is a prostitute's fee. In 2:12 the wife says of her vines and fig trees, "my pay, the gifts of my lovers", and the LORD answers that they were his gifts all along. Hosea 9:1 repeats the charge at the harvest. The threshing floor was where the grain was beaten out, measured and shared, and where a harvest feast was held. To the farmer the heap of grain looked like a wage from the god who made rain fall. Deuteronomy 23:18 forbids bringing "the pay of a prostitute" into the house of the LORD to pay a vow. Hosea says the whole harvest is that kind of money.

p: Food from a foreign land was thought to be unclean for the LORD's people. Ezekiel says the same of the exiles.
b: In Assyria the Israelites will eat food not prepared by the rules of clean and unclean (Leviticus 11) and not offered to the LORD. Ezekiel, speaking to Judean exiles, says the same: "This is how the Israelites will eat their bread, unclean, among the nations where I will drive them." (Ezekiel 4:13). The point is not only diet. A people cut off from the land and the sanctuary cannot keep the festivals (9:4-5), and the daily bread of exile is a sign of that loss. The verse also gives the people's two destinations: Egypt (the old house of slavery) and Assyria (the new one). See also Daniel 1:8-16 for the same worry about food in a later exile.
r: Ezekiel 4:13; Leviticus 11:1-47; Hosea 8:13; Hosea 9:6; Hosea 11:5; Daniel 1:8

p: Food in a house of death made the eater unclean. Offerings were not allowed to be eaten in that state.
b: A house where someone had died was unclean for seven days, and so was everything in it (Numbers 19:14-16). In Deuteronomy 26:14 a worshiper declares that he has not eaten the tithe "in my mourning", because food eaten in mourning could not be brought to the LORD. Hosea 9:4 says that Israel's bread will be like that: unfit for the LORD's house, only for the eater's own hunger. A related picture: the land of Assyria would be one great house of the dead, where nothing eaten was fit for worship. The verse also says that the wine offering will stop, and with it the festival (9:5).

p: The 'appointed festival' and 'feast of the LORD' point to the harvest gathering, later called Booths.
b: The Hebrew mo'ed is any fixed festival and chag a pilgrim feast. In an agricultural year the great feast was the autumn gathering at the end of the harvest (Exodus 23:16; Leviticus 23:39-43), when wine, oil and grain were brought in. The northern kingdom kept its own date for it: Jeroboam I "made a festival in the eighth month" at Bethel (1 Kings 12:32-33). Hosea 9:1-6 reads like a speech given at that gathering, when the people were glad about the crop and Hosea tells them to stop rejoicing. The next verses spell out why: in exile there will be no pouring of wine, no festival, no house of the LORD to go to.
orig: יוֹם מוֹעֵד / יוֹם חַג־יְהוָה (yom mo'ed / yom chag YHWH)

t: Memphis, the Egyptian city of the dead
p: The Hebrew name is Moph (Noph). The burial ground of Memphis was the great cemetery of Egypt.
b: Memphis, called Noph or Moph in Hebrew, was the old capital of Egypt, south of modern Cairo. Its great cemetery was at Saqqara, where the early pyramids stand. The line "Memphis will bury them" turns the city's reputation into a threat: those who run to Egypt for safety will die there and be buried in its graves. Judean refugees were living in Memphis in Jeremiah's time: "in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and the land of Pathros" (Jeremiah 44:1). The Greek of this verse names the burial place "Machmas" (Machmas), a different word from the Hebrew.

t: Who says the prophet is a fool?
p: The words may be the people's taunt, Hosea's bitter echo of it, or his description of false prophets.
b: The verse has no marks of speech. Three readings: (1) The people's taunt: when judgment comes they call the prophet crazy, as the officers of Jehu called the young prophet "that madman" (2 Kings 9:11: "What did that madman want with you?"). Most commentators take the line this way. (2) Hosea's own words about the prophets of Samaria, who are fools for promising peace (compare 4:5; Micah 2:11). (3) A statement of what the day of punishment will show: the one who is called mad will be proved right. The phrase "the man of the spirit" (ish haruach) is not a standard title; it means someone possessed by a spirit, in an honored or a mocking sense. The Plain leaves the sentence without quotation marks so that the three readings stay open.
orig: אֱוִיל הַנָּבִיא מְשֻׁגָּע אִישׁ הָרוּחַ ('evil hannavi meshugga' ish haruach)

a: A watchman for Ephraim, along with my God, is the prophet.
p: The Hebrew is very hard. The prophet is a watchman, and also a target.
b: A word-for-word line reads: "A watchman, Ephraim, with my God, a prophet; a fowler's snare on all his ways." It has been read: (1) The prophet is the watchman of Ephraim, on God's behalf, yet a snare lies on all his paths (the Plain follows this; compare Ezekiel 3:17: "I have set you as a watchman for the house of Israel."). (2) Ephraim is the watchman, waiting for God's word, and the prophet is a trap (a false prophet who misleads, as in Jeremiah 6:17). (3) Others divide the verse at "with my God" and make the prophet himself the snare. The "hostility in the house of his God" repeats the word of 9:7: the prophet is attacked in the very place where he speaks.
orig: צֹפֶה אֶפְרַיִם עִם־אֱלֹהָי נָבִיא (tsofeh Efrayim im-elohai navi)

t: Gibeah: the crime that became a byword
p: The story is in Judges 19-21. Hosea names it three times.
b: In Judges 19 men of Gibeah in Benjamin attacked a Levite's guest house and abused and killed his concubine; the other tribes went to war against Benjamin and nearly wiped it out. The response of the tribes at the time: "Nothing like this has been done or seen from the day the Israelites came up from the land of Egypt to this day." (Judges 19:30). Hosea uses Gibeah as the standard for depravity (9:9; 10:9) and as a place of alarm (5:8). Two other readings of "the days of Gibeah": the days of Saul's Gibeah, when Israel first asked for a king (1 Samuel 10:26; 11:4; compare Hosea 13:10-11), or a vague "olden days". The first is the plain one. The story had been told in Judges for generations before Hosea.
r: Judges 19:30; Judges 19:22; Judges 20:48; Hosea 5:8; Hosea 10:9; 1 Samuel 10:26

a: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness.
t: The wilderness as a first love
p: Israel at the start was a delight to the LORD. The same picture is in Jeremiah 2 and Deuteronomy 32.
b: Grapes in the desert and the first fig of the season are the surprise of an unexpected treat. The LORD "found" Israel in the wilderness: "He came upon him in a wilderness land, in a waste where the wild winds howl." (Deuteronomy 32:10). Jeremiah says it of Israel as a bride and a first harvest: "Israel was a holy thing for the LORD, the first of his produce." (Jeremiah 2:3). Hosea elsewhere pictures the wilderness as a place of new beginning (2:14-15; 13:5). The line here belongs to a different movement: Israel was a joy at first, and it was at the very next stop, Baal of Peor, that the turn came. The "ancestors" are the wilderness generation, as they are in 10:9 for the later "days of Gibeah".

p: The first disaster after the Exodus generation reached the Jordan: the worship of Moab's god at Peor.
b: At Shittim, east of the Jordan, "the people began to commit sexual sin with the daughters of Moab." (Numbers 25:1). "The women invited the people to the sacrifices for their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods." (Numbers 25:2). The text goes on: "So Israel tied itself to the Baal of Peor, and the LORD burned with anger against Israel." (Numbers 25:3). Psalm 106:28 recalls it and Deuteronomy 4:3 uses it as a warning. Peor is a mountain or a place in Moab; "Baal" is a title, "lord", used of local gods. Hosea sees in it the pattern of Israel's whole history: the people were chosen and delighted in, and as soon as they met the local religion they joined it.

p: The Hebrew word is bosheth, 'shame'. Scribes used it as a replacement for the name Baal.
b: Bosheth is "shame". In the Hebrew Bible the name Baal was often replaced by "shame" when a person bore a name with Baal in it: Ish-bosheth for Ish-baal (2 Samuel 2:8; 1 Chronicles 8:33), Mephibosheth for Merib-baal (2 Samuel 4:4; 1 Chronicles 8:34). Jeremiah calls Baal "the Shameful Thing" (Jeremiah 3:24; 11:13), and the Plain uses the same words here. The sense is not "shameful to look at" but "the one who brings shame on those who trust in him". The sentence says that they gave themselves to a shame and became what they loved.

a: Ephraim: their glory will fly away like a bird
p: The name Ephraim sounds like 'fruitful'. The next verses take away every fruit.
b: When Joseph's second son was born he named him Ephraim, "because God has made me fruitful in the land of my suffering." (Genesis 41:52). Hosea plays on that name in 9:11-16: the "glory" (the number of the people) flies like a bird, with no birth, no womb, no conception; the children will be killed (9:13); the womb will miscarry (9:14); the root is withered and they "will bear no fruit" (9:16). The hope of the name is reversed. Deuteronomy 28:4 and Genesis 49:25 had promised the blessing of "womb and breasts". Hosea 14:8 turns it back again: "your fruit comes from me." The threat is not that Ephraim will vanish in a day, but that each year there will be fewer.
r: Genesis 41:52; Genesis 49:25; Deuteronomy 28:4; Hosea 9:16; Hosea 13:15; Hosea 14:8

t: A prayer that turns a blessing into a curse
p: The prophet asks for barrenness for the people. Jesus quotes the idea on the way to the cross.
b: The prophet's role was to ask the LORD to spare the people (Amos 7:2, 5), and here he asks, grimly, for what the LORD has already said he will do. The line "Give them, LORD. What will you give?" shows him arguing back and forth with himself, as in Jeremiah 18:21. Luke puts the theme on the lips of Jesus: "For look, days are coming when people will say, 'Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never gave birth and breasts that never fed a baby.'" (Luke 23:29), followed in the next verse by Hosea 10:8. A reader should note that the prophet does not ask for it with joy; the next verse shows the LORD's own pain (11:8).

a: All their evil is at Gilgal.
p: Israel's first camp in Canaan, and a shrine in Hosea's day. Why 'there I came to hate them'? It is not clear.
b: Gilgal was where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:19-20) and where Saul was made king (1 Samuel 11:14-15). By the eighth century it was a shrine of the northern kingdom, condemned by Hosea (4:15; 12:11) and by Amos (4:4; 5:5). The reason for "there I came to hate them" is debated: (1) the present worship at Gilgal; (2) the making of Saul king there (1 Samuel 11:15), which fits Hosea's hostile view of kingship (13:10-11); (3) a general word for the sanctuary of the whole region. Only here in Hosea, and in Jeremiah 12:8, does the LORD say he hates his own people (compare Malachi 1:3 for Esau). It is the lowest point in the book, followed by "I will love them no more".
r: Joshua 4:19; 1 Samuel 11:14-15; Hosea 4:15; Hosea 12:11; Amos 4:4; Amos 5:5

a: I will love them no more.
p: The only place where the LORD says he will stop loving Israel. The book later reverses it.
b: The words are the harshest in the book. The LORD "will love them no more" and drives them out of "my house" (the land and the household, see 8:1). They should be read with the verse at the end of the book, "I will love them freely" (14:4), and with the LORD's inner struggle in 11:8-9. Three readings: (1) Time: the love stops for a period of exile and starts again; (2) Kind: the love that gave without limit becomes a love that disciplines; (3) Editorial: the chapters come from different times in Hosea's life, and the later hope answers the earlier despair. In Hosea 1:6 the name Lo-ruhamah, "Not Shown Compassion", already says the LORD will no longer have compassion.

t: A luxuriant, empty or plundering vine?
p: The Hebrew boqeq has three possible meanings. The Greek says 'fruitful'.
b: Israel is often a vine: "A vine from Egypt you dug up and moved." (Psalm 80:8); "But I planted you as a choice vine," (Jeremiah 2:21); and the vineyard song of Isaiah 5:1-7. The Hebrew adjective boqeq is the problem. It comes from baqaq, which means "to empty out" (Isaiah 24:1, 3) and "to plunder" (Nahum 2:2). Three readings: (1) Luxuriant, spreading, a vine that runs wild (the Plain, as the Greek euklematousa and most modern versions); (2) Empty, a vine that has run to leaves and no fruit, supported by the related verb; (3) Plundering, a vine that devours its own fruit. The next clause ("it bears fruit for itself") fits the first two. See the topic on the vine. The scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves the words gefen boqeq Yisra'el with nothing restored, so the Hebrew word is old; the Greek chose a sense for it. See the variant.
r: Psalm 80:8; Jeremiah 2:21; Isaiah 5:1-7; Isaiah 27:2; Nahum 2:2; Ezekiel 19:10

p: The pillars were standing stones set up at shrines. The Torah forbids them. Hosea names them again at 3:4.
b: A matsevah is an upright stone set up at a sacred place, as Jacob set up one at Bethel (Genesis 28:22). Many Israelites saw them as memorials to the LORD. Deuteronomy 16:22 forbids them ("You are not to set up a pillar") and Hosea treats them as part of the Baal cult. The part of the book already written has "no pillar" in the list at 3:4. Here the pillars get better as the land gets better: the richer the farmer, the finer the stone. The verse is about the use of prosperity. For the Canaanite practice and the later ban see the topic on standing stones.

p: The Hebrew can mean 'smooth, slippery' (false) or 'divided' (split between two loyalties). The Greek reads 'divided'.
b: Chalaq means "smooth". Smooth speech is flattery (Psalm 12:2; Proverbs 28:23), so a smooth heart can be a false one. The Greek says "They have divided their hearts" (emerisan), and many commentators take the Hebrew as "divided", from chalaq II, "divide": a heart split between the LORD and Baal. The Plain's "slippery" lets both readings stand: a heart that cannot be held. The next words (ye'shamu) can mean "they must bear their guilt" or "they are found guilty" (the Plain's choice).

a: break the necks of their altars
t: Breaking the neck: the law of the unwanted animal
p: The verb 'araf is used for breaking an animal's neck. The altars are treated like a donkey no one ransomed.
b: The verb 'araf appears in two Torah rulings. A donkey's firstborn that is not ransomed with a lamb has its neck broken: "If you do not ransom it, break its neck." (Exodus 13:13). And in the case of an unsolved murder the elders break the neck of a heifer in a wadi: "There in the valley they are to break the cow's neck." (Deuteronomy 21:4). In Hosea the LORD does to the altars what is done to an unredeemed animal or to the animal that stands for an unsolved crime. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIg spells the verb with a full vowel letter and agrees with the Masoretic Text.

t: When did they say 'We have no king'?
p: Possible occasions: the gaps after murdered kings, or the years after Hoshea was jailed.
b: The sentence looks to a day when there is no king to blame or to trust. Views: (1) the gaps after the murders in the 740s and 730s (2 Kings 15), (2) the years 724-722, when Hoshea had been arrested: "So the king of Assyria shut him up and bound him in a prison house." (2 Kings 17:4), and Samaria stood under siege with no king at its head, and (3) a proverb-like saying about a time to come. The words do not praise or blame kingship in themselves; the people know their king is gone because "we did not fear the LORD", and the second half asks what any king could do. Hosea 3:4 and 13:10-11 return to the same theme.

a: justice sprouts like a poison weed
p: The word for justice, mishpat, is the thing that grows as a weed. Amos says the same.
b: Mishpat, "justice", is what a king and a court owe the poor. In this verse the courts and treaties are so full of false oaths that justice itself grows like a weed in a plowed field. The weed (rosh) is a bitter, poisonous plant, perhaps hemlock or wormwood. Amos 6:12 says of the northern leaders: "Yet you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood." The "covenants" are the treaties with Assyria and Egypt (7:11; 12:1) and also contracts and oaths between neighbors. A different reading takes mishpat as "judgment" or "lawsuit": a legal case grows up in the field of the covenant, as in Hosea 12:2.

p: Hosea twists the name of Bethel, 'house of God', into 'house of wickedness' or 'house of nothing'.
b: Hosea changes Beth-el ("house of God") to Beth-aven ("house of wickedness" or "of nothing"), here and at 4:15 and 5:8. There was also a real Beth-aven near Ai (Joshua 7:2), and the geography is debated, but in Hosea the name is nearly always a play on Bethel. The Greek has "Beth-On" (oikos On), which turns the name into the Egyptian city On (Heliopolis). The word kemarim (the Plain's "idol priests") is used for priests of other gods and of image-worship (2 Kings 23:5; Zephaniah 1:4). The "glory" of Samaria is probably the calf itself, taken as tribute by Assyria in the next verse.

p: Conquerors carried off the images of the gods they beat. 'King Jareb' appears also at 5:13.
b: Assyrian kings routinely took the images of the gods of conquered cities to Nineveh or Calah, as their own inscriptions say (Hallo, Context of Scripture); Sargon II's account of the fall of Samaria is usually read as saying the same. For Hosea the calf is carried to Assyria like a hostage, a "gift" (minchah) to the great king, who will not worship it. "King Jareb" (also 5:13) is not named in Assyrian records; yareb may be "the contending one", or perhaps a Hebrew rendering of the title "great king" (Akkadian sharru rabu), and some take it as the personal name of an unknown person. The Plain keeps it as a name and notes the doubt. The scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves "to King Jareb" with nothing restored; the Greek writes "Iareim". See the variant.

a: like a twig on the water's surface
p: The Hebrew qetsef has been read as 'twig' (the Greek) and 'foam' (Jerome's Latin).
b: Qetsef elsewhere means "anger", but that cannot be right for a king floating on water. The Greek has phryganon, "a dry twig, brushwood", and the Plain follows it. Jerome's Latin (the Vulgate) has spuma, "foam", and many later readers follow it. A third reading, "splinter", would suit the cult-image of 8:6. A twig on a river, a piece of foam on a pond: either way the picture is of something carried away, helpless. The verb nidmeh (the Plain's "will be destroyed") is from a root meaning "cut off", and is repeated at the end of the chapter. The scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves "like qetsef on the face of the water" with the word itself unrestored, so the consonants are old.

t: 'Cover us!' on the road to the cross and at the end of the world
p: Hosea 10:8 is quoted by Jesus in Luke 23:30 and echoed in Revelation 6:16.
b: On the way to the cross Jesus says: "That is when they will start telling the mountains, 'Fall on us,' and the hills, 'Cover us.'" (Luke 23:30). The order is reversed from Hosea's (cover, then fall); the Greek of Hosea keeps Hosea's order, so the swap is Luke's. In Revelation the peoples of the earth say it at the sixth seal, crying to the mountains and the rocks, 'Fall on us! Hide us from the face of the one who sits on the throne' (Revelation 6:16). Isaiah 2:19-21 has the same flight into caves. In Hosea the cry belongs to the fall of Samaria's shrines; in Luke it is a warning of Jerusalem's coming fall, and in Revelation it is the end of the age.

a: Thorn and thistle will grow up
p: The curse of Genesis 3 falls on the altars.
b: The two plants, qots and dardar, are those of the curse on the ground: "Thorn and thistle it will sprout for you," (Genesis 3:18). Here they cover the altars, and the first reader would hear the curse of the garden fall on the cult places. In Isaiah 5:6 the abandoned vineyard also grows "thorns and thistles".

p: The Hebrew has 'their two iniquities'. A margin note and the Greek differ.
b: Candidates: (1) the two calves, at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:29); (2) the sins of Gibeah and of the calf in 10:5-9, the old and the new; (3) two kinds of sin, worship and politics; (4) the sins of the two kingdoms, Ephraim and Judah. The text written in the line (the Ketiv) has "their two eyes", and the reading in the margin (the Qere) is "their two iniquities"; the Greek also has "two iniquities". Some propose "their two furrows" by changing a letter, to fit the plowing picture of 10:11. The verb be'osram can mean "when I bind them", as the Plain's "bound". See the variant.

t: A heifer that loved to thresh
p: Threshing is easy work for an ox: it eats as it treads. Plowing is not.
b: A threshing ox was not muzzled (Deuteronomy 25:4), so threshing was an animal's easy work, eating while it trod. Plowing and harrowing were a hard yoke. The LORD says that Ephraim, trained and comfortable, was spared the hard work and now will pull. 4:16 had called Ephraim "as stubborn as a heifer", and Jeremiah has Ephraim say "like a calf that was never trained" (Jeremiah 31:18); the Plain's phrase "trained" and "never trained" are two sides of the same picture. In the end of the verse Judah plows and Jacob harrows: the work falls on the whole people, north and south.

p: A call to turn: 'sow' and 'reap' come from 8:7 and 10:13 and turn the other way.
b: The agricultural pictures of the chapter are turned to a plain call. In 8:7 the people sowed wind and reaped a storm; in 10:13 they plowed wickedness and reaped injustice; here they are told to sow righteousness and reap by the measure of loyal love. The Greek has a different text: "Sow for yourselves in righteousness, harvest the fruit of life, light for yourselves the light of knowledge." The phrase "loyal love" (hesed) and "justice" belong together in Hosea (2:19; 6:6; 12:6). "Plow new ground" (the Plain) is a call to break up the unused soil and make a fresh start, not to stay on the hardened field.
r: Hosea 8:7; Hosea 10:13; Hosea 2:19; Hosea 6:6; Hosea 12:6; Proverbs 11:18

p: The Hebrew yoreh means 'rain on' and also 'teach'. Joel 2:23 plays on the same two senses.
b: The verb yarah in this form can be "he will rain" (from the rain called yoreh, the early rain) or "he will teach" (as in torah, "teaching"). The Plain takes "rains", fitting the sowing picture. Jewish and Christian readers have often heard both: God sends the rain of righteousness and teaches it. Joel 2:23 plays on the same two senses, and Hosea 6:3 compares the LORD's coming to "the spring rain". A reader hears that righteousness is not something the farmer grows by himself; it comes down as a gift on the one who has plowed.

a: when a mother was smashed with her children
t: The horror of an old war
p: Mothers dashed with their children: a war crime told as a past event, and used again in 13:16.
b: The Hebrew is "mother with children was dashed", the same verb ratash that Hosea uses for the coming fall of Samaria: "Their little ones will be smashed" (13:16). The same atrocity is named in 2 Kings 8:12 (Elisha's tears for what Hazael will do), Isaiah 13:16, Nahum 3:10 and Psalm 137:9. The verse expects the hearer to know the event of Shalman and Beth-arbel; we do not. The Plain gives the line as told, without softening it: this is how war was fought, and Hosea uses it as a comparison, not as an order. Compare 13:16 and the note there.

t: Who was Shalman, and where was Beth-arbel?
p: Nobody knows. The suggestions: Shalmaneser V, Salamanu of Moab, or an unknown raid.
b: Suggestions: (1) Shalmaneser V, the Assyrian king at the fall of Samaria (726-722 BC), whose name Hosea shortens; (2) Salamanu of Moab, named in the tribute lists of Tiglath-pileser III, linked with Hosea's line on the guess that he raided Gilead; (3) Zalmunna, the Midianite king of Judges 8:5-21, with the verse recalling an old defeat; (4) a raid we know nothing about. Beth-arbel is possibly Arbela in Galilee near the lake or Irbid in Gilead. The Greek gives a different line: "like Salaman, a ruler from the house of Jeroboam", reading Beth-arbel as Beth-Jeroboam. See the variant.

a: At dawn the king of Israel
p: The words are near the opening of the Greek's chapter 11, because the Greek divides the verse differently.
b: The Hebrew nidmo nidmah is an emphatic form: "he will be utterly cut off". The Greek begins 11:1 with the words "At dawn they were cast off; the king of Israel was cast off", so it puts these words at the start of the next chapter. English and Hebrew both keep them at the end of 10:15. "At dawn" can mean the early morning of the invasion, or "suddenly", or the dawn of the day of the LORD; Hosea 6:3 also speaks of the dawn. The king in view may be Hoshea, taken before Samaria fell (2 Kings 17:4).

a: When Israel was a youth, I loved him
t: A youth, a boy, a child?
p: The Hebrew na'ar is a young person, not a baby. The chapter pictures Israel as a growing boy.
b: Na'ar covers a boy and a young man, a person old enough to be called but young enough to be taught. The LORD's words to Pharaoh already call the nation a son: "Israel is my son, my firstborn." (Exodus 4:22). Hosea gives the story its tenderness: the LORD loved him, called him, taught him to walk (11:3) and fed him (11:4). Few passages in the Old Testament tell the Exodus so fully from the side of a parent's love; compare Deuteronomy 1:31 and 32:10-12. Jeremiah 31:9 and Deuteronomy 14:1 use the same family language. The verb "loved" is the one used for the love of a husband in chapters 1-3 and for the choice of Israel in Deuteronomy 7:7-8.
r: Exodus 4:22; Deuteronomy 14:1; Deuteronomy 7:7-8; Jeremiah 31:9; Hosea 3:1; Deuteronomy 1:31; Deuteronomy 32:10-12

t: "Out of Egypt I called my son": Hosea and Matthew
p: Matthew applies the line to Jesus. The Hebrew and the Greek of Hosea differ, and Matthew follows the Hebrew.
b: Matthew says Joseph's stay in Egypt happened "so that what the Lord spoke through the prophet would be fulfilled: 'Out of Egypt I called my son.'" (Matthew 2:15). In Hosea the line is about the Exodus: the son is Israel. Views of Matthew's use: (1) typology: Israel's story is a pattern that Jesus, the true Son, repeats, so Matthew finds the pattern "filled" in him (the commonest view); (2) prophecy: the line was always about the Messiah, a rare reading today; (3) application: Matthew uses a familiar line as a fit description, without claiming Hosea predicted it; (4) Jewish interpretive method, reading the Bible's patterns the way Matthew's contemporaries did. The Greek of Hosea reads "his children" (see the variant), so Matthew translated the Hebrew himself or used another text. Jerome noticed this. See the card below.

a: I held them up by their arms
t: The parent who carries a child
p: The LORD as father and nurse carrying Israel through the wilderness.
b: The picture is of a parent steadying a toddler with a hand under each arm. Moses uses the same one: "...the LORD your God carried you, the way a man carries his son, all along the road you traveled until you came to this place." (Deuteronomy 1:31). Isaiah 46:3-4 and Numbers 11:12 speak of the LORD carrying and nursing the people. The Greek translator took the first verb differently (see the variant) and wrote that the LORD bound Ephraim's feet. The last line, "they did not know that I healed them", sets up the rest of the book's use of healing: the LORD is the healer (6:1; 7:1; 14:4) while Ephraim looks for healing in Assyria (5:13).
r: Deuteronomy 1:31; Isaiah 46:3-4; Numbers 11:12; Hosea 5:13; Hosea 6:1; Hosea 14:4

p: The cords are the ropes a person uses to lead an animal, made gentle.
b: Chavle adam, "cords of a human", are the ropes a farmer uses to lead and guide, not to drag. Some read it as "human cords", ropes of the kind used by people (the Plain), others as "cords of kindness" (where adam carries the sense of human feeling), others as "cords of Adam", for the bond between the LORD and the human race. The next phrase, "ropes of love", uses 'avot, a thick rope. Greek has "I stretched them out in the bonds of my love". The point is that the pull is the pull of love, not of force. The second half of the verse turns the same animal-handling picture.

a: lift the yoke off their jaws
p: The Hebrew al may be 'on' or 'off'; some read 'infant' (ul) for 'yoke' (ol).
b: Two problems. (1) The line says the LORD was "like those who lift the yoke 'al their jaws". The preposition can mean "on" or "off": the Plain takes "off", as a farmer eases the yoke so an ox can eat (and compare Leviticus 26:13: "I broke the bars of your yoke and made you walk upright."). Others take it as "lift a yoke up on their jaws", the tight picture. (2) A few suggest reading 'ul, "infant", for 'ol, "yoke", giving "those who lift an infant to their cheeks", a parent's kiss. The consonants are the same (the scroll 4QXIIg writes the full form of "yoke"). The Plain keeps "yoke". Either way the LORD is gentle: the strain is eased and food is given.
orig: כְּמֵרִימֵי עֹל עַל לֶחֱיֵיהֶם (kemerimei ol al lechyehem)

a: because they refused to turn back
t: Return and return: Egypt and the LORD
p: One verb, shuv, sits at both ends: not back to Egypt, yet they refused to turn back.
b: Shuv is "turn back, return", and it carries the book's main word-play. "Return to Egypt" (8:13; 9:3) is the curse of the exile; "return to the LORD" is the repentance Hosea asks for (6:1; 14:1-2). The first shuv of this verse is negative: they will not go back to Egypt; the second says why: they refused to turn back to the LORD (the Plain uses "turn back" for repentance and "return" for going back to a place). The effect is that a people who will not turn back to God will be forced to turn to a foreign power. The word lo at the head of the verse can also mean a question ("Will they not return to Egypt?"), as many commentators read. See the variant for the Greek, which says they "lived in Egypt".
orig: לֹא יָשׁוּב ... מֵאֲנוּ לָשׁוּב (lo yashuv ... me'anu lashuv)

a: break the bars of their gates
p: The Hebrew baddav can be 'his bars' or 'his boasters'.
b: The word baddim means bars (as in Job 17:16, the bars of Sheol) or "empty talkers, boasters" (Isaiah 44:25; Jeremiah 50:36, where it names diviners). The Plain takes bars: a sword that breaks the gate bars lets the enemy in. If the other meaning is right, the sword would silence the empty-talking prophets and counselors, which fits the last phrase, "because of their own schemes" (mo'atsot, "counsels"). The Greek has "it grew weak in their cities and rested in their hands", an entirely different line.

p: The Hebrew al can be a name, 'Most High', or 'upward'. 7:16 has a related line.
b: The Hebrew says: "To 'al they call him, together he does not lift". 'Al means "up, above". Readings: (1) a name, "to the One Above" or "to the Most High" ('Elyon), who is the LORD (the Plain); (2) "upward", so the call is a call to go up, which none will do (compare 7:16: "They turn, but not upward."); (3) a god: they call to Baal as "the one above". The second half of the verse also can be read two ways: "he will not lift them" (the LORD), or "no one lifts them" (the idol cannot). The Plain's "none of them will be lifted up" keeps both. The chapter's turn from judgment to love begins right after this verse.

a: My heart turns over inside me
p: The verb hafak is the one used for the overthrow of Sodom. The LORD's heart is overturned instead of the city.
b: The Hebrew nehpakh is from hafakh, "overturn", the standard verb for the destruction of Sodom: "He overthrew those cities and the whole plain" (Genesis 19:25). Admah and Zeboiim were two of the cities of the plain that shared the fate: "Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and rage." (Deuteronomy 29:23). Lamentations 4:6 says Sodom "was overturned in a moment". Hosea has the LORD refuse to treat Ephraim as he treated those cities, because his own heart is "overturned": the upheaval that would have fallen on Ephraim falls on him. The Plain keeps "turns over" so the link with Sodom's "overturning" can be seen. The topic page on God's regret treats the verse beside Genesis 6:6 and 1 Samuel 15.
r: Genesis 19:25; Deuteronomy 29:23; Genesis 14:2; Lamentations 4:6; Jeremiah 31:20; Isaiah 63:15

p: The Hebrew uses the verb for a deep stirring of feeling, as when Joseph saw his brother.
b: The noun is nichumim, from nacham, the root that also gives "comfort" and "relent", and the verb nikhmeru means "grow warm, be stirred". The same verb is used of Joseph when he sees Benjamin: his heart "burned with love for his brother" (Genesis 43:30), and of the real mother before Solomon, who felt her love "burning inside her" (1 Kings 3:26). Jeremiah's answer to Ephraim says: "So my insides churn for him; I will have mercy on him, I truly will, the LORD declares." (Jeremiah 31:20). The Plain uses "pity" for this root so that it differs from rachamim, "compassion" (the root of Lo-ruhamah, "Not Shown Compassion", 1:6), and the root's link to "relent" can be explained in the note on God's regret.

a: I am God, not a human being
t: God is not a man: and yet his heart turns
p: God says he is not a human being, in the same breath that he shows feelings.
b: Two earlier texts use the same words, both in the context of whether God changes: "God is not a man, that he should lie, or a human being, that he should change his mind." (Numbers 23:19), and "Also, Israel's Enduring One does not lie and does not regret. He is not a human being, to have regrets." (1 Samuel 15:29). Hosea's sentence may be read in three ways. (1) God does not carry out his anger because he is not like a human who loses his temper: human anger takes revenge, divine holiness does not. (2) God's refusal to destroy is not a change of mind but the steadiness of his love. (3) The verse shows that the LORD feels, and that his "not changing" means he does not change his loyalty, not that he lacks feeling. The card below sets the traditions side by side.

a: I will not enter in rage
p: The Hebrew be'ir is 'in a city' or 'in rage'. The Greek and Jerome read 'city'.
b: The Hebrew ba'ir is written like "in a city". If "city" is meant, the LORD says "I will not come into the city" (as the Greek has it: "I will not enter into a city"; so does Jerome's Latin), perhaps meaning he will not enter Ephraim's city as a destroyer, or that he does not dwell in a city but among the people. The other reading takes the same consonants as a rare word for "anger, rage" ('ir, from a root meaning "be aroused"), matching "burning anger" in the line before. The Plain takes "rage", which fits best with the parallel lines. The phrase "the Holy One among you" is also the language of Isaiah 12:6.

t: The lion that calls them home
p: Hosea has used the lion as a threat (5:14; 13:7). Here the lion's roar brings the children home.
b: In 5:14 the LORD is "like a lion to Ephraim", in 13:7 he is a lion by the road, and in 13:8 a lioness. Here the same animal roars, and the response is not flight but a return: the children "come shaking from the west". Amos had said "The LORD roars from Zion" (Amos 1:2) and "A lion has roared. Who is not afraid?" (Amos 3:8). Hosea turns the roar. The trembling is a mix of fear and hurry (the same verb, charad, describes both). In 11:11 the birds from Egypt and the dove from Assyria echo the places of the exile in 8:13 and 9:3: the exile is undone, but by a call, not a march.

a: Ephraim has ringed me round with lying
p: English 11:12 is the first verse of Hebrew chapter 12. English 12:1-14 are Hebrew 12:2-15.
b: The Hebrew Bible starts its chapter 12 at the verse the English calls 11:12. So English 11:12 = Hebrew 12:1, and English 12:1-14 = Hebrew 12:2-15. The Plain, notes and references on this site use the English numbers throughout. The Greek (Rahlfs, Swete) follows the English here (its 11:12 is the line that begins "Ephraim has surrounded me..."). The same shift happens at the end of Hosea: English 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1, and English 14:1-9 is Hebrew 14:2-10. Anyone reading a Jewish commentary or a Hebrew Bible should add one to the English verse number from 12:1 to 12:14, and one from 14:1 to 14:9, and move 13:16 to 14:1.

p: The Hebrew can say that Judah still walks with God, or that he still runs wild against him.
b: The verb rad is rare. It may come from rud, "roam freely", which can be good (free to walk with God) or bad (unruly). The two readings: (1) praise, "Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One" (older Jewish commentators, KJV and some moderns), a contrast with Ephraim's lies; (2) blame, "Judah is still unruly against God, against the faithful Holy One", which matches 12:2, where the LORD has a case against Judah, and "Judah" is warned also in 4:15 and 5:5. The Greek has a different line (see the variant). The Plain's "roams with God" holds both: Judah is not simply in the right. The word qedoshim, "holy ones", is plural in form; it can be a plural of majesty for God ("the Holy One"), or refer to the angels or to the saints.

p: The Hebrew verb is 'shepherd', not 'feed on'. Wind is the book's word for emptiness.
b: The verb is ro'eh, from the root "shepherd, graze". The old English "feeds on the wind" takes it as "grazes on", and the Plain says "herds the wind", which keeps the picture of a shepherd trying to drive something that cannot be driven. The wind is a Hosea image for the useless thing (8:7; 13:15) and the "east wind" (qadim) is the hot, dry wind off the desert that scorches crops (13:15). Ecclesiastes uses the same picture in its own way: "chasing the wind". The line is about the ruinous foreign policy of the next lines. The verse number note: English 12:1 is Hebrew 12:2 (see 11:12).

a: olive oil is taken to Egypt
p: Oil was a gift that sealed a treaty or bought a favor.
b: Olive oil was a main export of the hill country and a typical gift to a king (Isaiah 57:9). Taking oil to Egypt while cutting a covenant with Assyria is Hosea's picture of playing both sides, which is what the last king did: Hoshea paid tribute to Assyria and "had sent messengers to So king of Egypt" (2 Kings 17:4). Hosea 7:11 says the same: "They have called to Egypt; they have gone off to Assyria." The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) is transcribed with no word for "and oil" in this line, between "they make" and "to Egypt"; whether this is an omission or only a gap in the transcription cannot be told from the printout, so the Plain keeps the Masoretic Text and the Greek, which both have the oil.

t: The case against Judah, and Jacob
p: The LORD brings a case against Judah and then against 'Jacob'. Jacob here is Ephraim, or the whole people.
b: The word rib is a legal case (4:1: "the LORD has a case against the people who live in the land"). Here Judah is named in the charge, which many critics think reflects a Judean reading of the book after 722 BC; others say Hosea addressed both kingdoms from the start (compare 5:5, 10; 6:4, 11; 8:14; 11:12). "Jacob" is the next name in the verse; it is a name for the people as the heir of the patriarch, and it sets up the pun in the verses that follow (heel-grabber, deceiver). Similar wording on repaying people for their deeds is in Jeremiah 25:14 and Ezekiel 36:19. Micah 6:1-8 is a lawsuit of the same kind, though there the LORD addresses "my people" and not the two kingdoms by name.
orig: רִיב לַיהוָה עִם־יְהוּדָה (riv laYHWH im Yehudah)

a: While still in the womb, he caught his brother's heel
p: Jacob's name means 'heel-grabber'. Hosea turns the birth scene into a fault or a mark of favor.
b: Genesis tells it this way: "Next his brother came out with his hand gripping Esau's heel, and he was named Jacob." (Genesis 25:26). Esau later said: "He has grabbed me by the heel these two times." (Genesis 27:36). The verb 'aqav can mean "take by the heel" and also "cheat, supplant". Hosea's line is read two ways. (1) As a charge: the people are as grasping as their ancestor, who cheated from before birth (the view in 12:2 that "the LORD punishes Jacob" fits this). (2) As a sign of favor: he took hold of things in God's plan from the womb, and the next lines (he struggled with God, he wept and begged) set him up as a model. Hosea may be playing on both. Jewish and Christian readers have held each reading.

a: He struggled against the angel and overcame him.
t: Angel and God: whom did Jacob wrestle?
p: Genesis 32 says 'a man'. Hosea says 'God' and 'angel' of the same wrestler, and adds that Jacob wept.
b: In Genesis "a man wrestled with him until the dawn came up" (Genesis 32:24), and Jacob's new name is explained: "for you have struggled with God and with humans and have won" (Genesis 32:28). Hosea 12:3-4 calls the opponent "God" and "the angel" in two lines, and says Jacob "wept and pleaded". Genesis does not mention tears: they may come from another form of the story, or from Hosea's reading of Genesis 32:26 ("I will not let you go unless you bless me"). On the identity: (1) the opponent was God appearing as an angel, the angel of the LORD; (2) it was an angel, and the Genesis "God" speaks for the sender; some church fathers took it as the Son before the incarnation. The Plain follows the Hebrew and does not decide.

p: Bethel is where Jacob dreamed of the stairway, and where God spoke with him again.
b: Jacob first met God at Bethel on the way out (Genesis 28:10-22), and God appeared again when he came back (Genesis 35:1-15): "To the place where God had spoken with him, Jacob gave the name Bethel." (Genesis 35:15). In Hosea Bethel is the shrine that he renames Beth-aven and tells the people not to go up to (4:15; 10:5, 15). Here it is the place of the ancestor's meeting with God, which the people's descendants have turned into a place of calves. The line "there he spoke with us" moves from the ancestor to the descendants: what God said to Jacob at Bethel was said to everyone who came after. The Hebrew "he found him" does not name its subject: most take God as finding Jacob, but the sentence can be turned the other way, and the same consonants can be read "he found us". The Plain keeps the open wording; the Greek has "they found me".

a: the LORD is his name to be remembered
t: The name by which he is called to mind
p: The same word zikhro is in Exodus 3:15. Hosea gives the full name, as against the names of the Baals.
b: In Exodus God gives Moses his name: "This is my name for all time, and by this name people will call me to mind, age after age." (Exodus 3:15). Hosea 12:5 uses the same word (zekher, "memorial, remembrance") and the name YHWH. The line stands between the Bethel scene and the call to turn back (12:6); it says that the God of Jacob's story is the LORD, God of Armies, and that his name is the name Israel is meant to remember. In 2:17 the LORD says he will take the names of the Baals from the people's lips so that they will not be remembered by name again. The Plain's "his name to be remembered" keeps the word "remember" at the end of the line.

a: But you must turn back to your God.
t: Turn back, with the help of your God
p: The Hebrew be-elohekha can mean 'by', 'in' or 'to'. The Plain keeps the plain call.
b: The sentence is in the Hebrew ve'attah be'lohekha tashuv: "and you, by/in your God, turn back". Readings: (1) "by the help of your God, return", so repentance is possible because God helps; (2) "return to your God", taking the preposition as "to"; (3) "you will return, in your God", a promise. The Plain takes the plain command. The verb shuv is the book's word for repentance and return (6:1; 14:1-2). "Loyal love and justice" is Hosea's summary of what God wants (2:19; 10:12; 6:6); Micah 6:8 states the same demand. "Wait for your God, always" matches the call to "seek the LORD" in 10:12.

p: The Hebrew kena'an is both 'Canaan' and 'trader'. Ephraim is called by the name of what he has become.
b: Kena'an is the name of the land and its people and, because the Canaanites (the Phoenicians) were the great traders, a word for "merchant" (Proverbs 31:24; Isaiah 23:8; Zephaniah 1:11). Hosea's sentence therefore means both: Ephraim is a Canaanite in his ways, and he is a merchant with cheating scales. Ezekiel makes the same insult: "Your roots and your birth come from the land of the Canaanites." (Ezekiel 16:3). Amos names the practice: "cheat with scales that lie" (Amos 8:5). Leviticus 19:35-36 and Deuteronomy 25:13-16 forbid false weights. The Plain keeps "Canaan" with the gloss "trader" so that the insult is not lost.
r: Ezekiel 16:3; Amos 8:5; Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16; Proverbs 11:1; Zephaniah 1:11

p: Ephraim says his wealth proves his innocence. The church in Laodicea says the same.
b: Ephraim reasons that earnings so large cannot have come from sin. The second half of the verse is a claim of innocence: "no one will find any guilt in me that counts as sin". The LORD's answer is the cheating scales of the previous verse. A reader of Revelation will hear the same boast: "You say, 'I am rich. I have grown wealthy, and I need nothing.' But you do not know that you are the one who is wretched and pitiful, poor, blind, and naked." (Revelation 3:17). The Hebrew word for "wealth" is on, which can also mean "strength, vigor"; it sounds almost like aven, "wickedness" (12:11), and Hosea's ear may have used the likeness.

a: Again I will settle you in tents
p: The LORD promises to put Israel back in tents. This could be punishment, restoration, or a festival.
b: Three readings. (1) Threat: the people will lose their houses and live in tents like refugees or wilderness wanderers (Hosea 2:14; 9:3). (2) Promise: the festival of Booths recalls the wilderness, and the verse promises it again (Hosea 2:14-15 pictures the wilderness as a place of betrothal). (3) Memory: the LORD recalls the joy of the first feast, as a contrast to the present. The law of Booths says: "Live in booths for seven days." (Leviticus 23:42), "so that your descendants will know that I made the Israelites live in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt." (Leviticus 23:43). The Plain's "as on festival days" keeps the link with the feast; it does not decide whether the sentence is judgment or hope. The opening words repeat 13:4.

a: through the prophets I spoke in comparisons
p: Prophets used pictures. The Hebrew 'adammeh may mean 'I told likenesses' or 'I made myself like'.
b: The LORD describes his way of speaking: to the prophets, with many visions, and through them "in comparisons" ('adammeh, from damah, "be like, compare"). This is the language of Numbers 12:6: "I make myself known to him in a vision" and of the later sentence in 2 Kings 17:13 that the LORD warned Israel "by every prophet and every visionary". The Greek has "I was made like" (homoiothen), reading the verb as "I was made similar" (the LORD took on forms). The sense of the Plain is that prophecy uses pictures and stories (like Hosea's marriage and the images of this book) to carry what plain speech could not. It sets up the sentence on Moses in 12:13.

p: Both place names sound like the word for a heap of stones.
b: Hosea plays on sound. Gal means a heap of stones. "Gilgal" begins with it, and so does "Gilead", which Genesis explains as the heap of stones set up by Jacob and Laban: "Laban said, 'This heap is a witness between me and you today.' That is why it was named Galeed," (Genesis 31:48). So the altars at Gilgal become gallim, heaps in a plowed field, the stones cleared off the soil. The effect: the altars are no better than a farmer's piles of rock, and Gilead, a place whose name means "heap of witness", is called wicked. "Gilead" in 6:8 (in the first part of the book) is the city of evildoers. Gilgal is condemned also in 4:15, 9:15 and Amos 4:4.

a: and for a wife he stood watch
p: Jacob 'kept watch' for a wife. The LORD 'kept watch' over Israel through a prophet.
b: The Hebrew repeats shamar in two senses: "keep, guard" (a flock) and "watch over, preserve". Jacob "fled to the country of Aram" (the region of Haran) and worked fourteen years for Rachel and Leah (Genesis 29:15-30), and for Laban's flocks six more (Genesis 30:25-31:41); the Hebrew leaves out "sheep", which the Plain also leaves out. Moses names the ancestor as "a wandering Aramean" (Deuteronomy 26:5). The Plain shows the pun by using "stood watch" in 12:12 and "was watched over" in 12:13. The contrast is between the ancestor, who served as a hired hand for a woman, and the nation, whom the LORD himself watched over by a prophet.

a: by a prophet the LORD brought Israel up out of Egypt
t: The prophet is Moses, never named
p: Hosea does not name Moses. He calls him 'a prophet', as Deuteronomy does.
b: Moses is not named anywhere in Hosea. Here he is "a prophet", the title Deuteronomy gives him: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers." (Deuteronomy 18:15), and the book ends by saying that no prophet since has arisen in Israel like Moses (Deuteronomy 34:10). The title fits Hosea's own job: Israel was brought out and kept safe by a prophet's word, and they now refuse one. Some scholars hold that the "prophet" is Moses and Hosea sees the whole prophetic line as his heirs; a few that the "prophet" is the line of prophets, since 12:10 spoke of them. The first reading is the plain one. The link of Jacob (12:12) with Moses (12:13) turns on a contrast: one fled, the other led the people out.

p: The Hebrew ritet is found nowhere else. 'Shudder' fits the context.
b: Ritet is a rare word, nowhere else in the Bible; the Greek has "judgments" (dikaiomata), the Latin "horror". "Trembling, shuddering" is the usual guess from a root meaning "tremble". The sentence is about Ephraim's standing: the tribe of Joshua and Jeroboam I, the tribe Jacob put before Manasseh (Genesis 48:19-20), whose word carried weight in Israel (compare Judges 8:1; 12:1, where Ephraim demanded to be heard). The Plain keeps the effect: when Ephraim spoke, people took notice. The point of the line is the fall that follows: such a tribe, "he died".

a: fell into guilt through Baal, and he died
p: The death may be spiritual, political or the future fall of the kingdom told as already happened.
b: Readings: (1) Spiritual death, the loss of life with God through Baal worship (compare Romans 6:23); (2) Political death, the loss of independence under Assyria, told in the past tense as the certain result (the prophetic perfect); (3) A past event, the Baal worship under Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 16:31-33), which Hosea sees as the beginning of the kingdom's end; Jehu's dynasty, which wiped out Ahab's house and its Baal worship (2 Kings 10:28), was still on the throne in Hosea's early years. The singular "he" is Ephraim as a person. Christian readers have also contrasted this "death" with the "life" of 14:5-7, and the resurrection language of 6:2 and 13:14.

a: Those who sacrifice human beings kiss calves
t: 'Kiss calves': sacrifice, human sacrifice, or both?
p: The Hebrew is hard. The Plain reads it as a statement: people who sacrifice humans kiss calves. The Greek has a very different line.
b: The Hebrew is zove'ei adam 'agalim yishaqun, literally "sacrificers of man, calves they kiss". The verb yishaqun is an imperfect, which can describe ("they kiss") or command ("let them kiss"), and adam can be what is sacrificed or the ones who sacrifice. Readings: (1) Human sacrifice: "Those who sacrifice human beings kiss calves" (the Plain); (2) People who sacrifice: "Men who offer sacrifices kiss calves", with no human victims, only the charge of calf-worship; (3) A taunt or a command: "Let the sacrificers kiss calves", Hosea's sarcasm or the people's own call. The Plain takes (1) as a description and adds no command. Human sacrifice is not named elsewhere in Hosea, but the Bible says Israel practiced child sacrifice (2 Kings 17:17: "They made their sons and their daughters pass through the fire."). Kissing is a sign of homage to an image: the LORD says that seven thousand in Israel have not bent to Baal or kissed him (1 Kings 19:18). Compare the variant, where the Greek reads an order to sacrifice people because the calves have run out.
orig: זֹבְחֵי אָדָם עֲגָלִים יִשָּׁקוּן (zove'ei adam 'agalim yishaqun)

a: like the dew that rises early and is gone
p: The morning cloud and early dew are the words of 6:4, where they describe the people's loyal love.
b: In 6:4 the LORD says to Ephraim and Judah: "Your loyal love is a morning cloud, dew that rises early and is gone." In 13:3 the same two pictures are used of the people themselves, and two more are added (chaff, smoke). The repeated words close the circle: the love that vanished like dew has taken the people with it. The pictures are of what is there at sunrise and gone by noon. The last pair is a pair of the lightest things in the farmyard and the house, chaff blown off the threshing floor by the wind and smoke leaving through a window. In 14:5 the LORD says "I will be like the dew to Israel", turning the same picture upside down.

p: In Hebrew 'know' covers choosing and caring, not only recognizing.
b: Yada' is "know" in the sense of a relationship. Amos has the LORD say of Israel: "You are the only ones I have known among all the clans of the earth." (Amos 3:2). Deuteronomy says of the wilderness years: "He knows every step of your journey through this huge wilderness." (Deuteronomy 2:7). The Greek translator wrote "I shepherded you" (epoimainon), and the Latin "I knew you". In Hosea the word is also in the setting of the lawsuit: the people have "no knowledge of God" (4:1) and "know no god" but the LORD (13:4), while he knew them in the desert. The rare word in the next line (tal'ubot, "drought, scorching") occurs only here.

a: Full, they let their hearts swell with pride.
p: Moses had warned that fullness leads to forgetting. Hosea says it happened.
b: Deuteronomy 8:12-14 sketches the danger: when you have eaten and are full and your herds multiply, "do not let your heart grow proud, so that you forget the LORD your God" (the sentence is in Deuteronomy 8:14: "Then do not let your heart grow proud, so that you forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves."). The Song of Moses says it with an animal: "Jeshurun grew fat, and he kicked;" (Deuteronomy 32:15). Hosea closes the circle: the pasture of the wilderness became the pasture of Canaan, and the fed child forgot the one who fed him. The structure of Hosea 13:1-6 is then a short history: speak, sin, die, Egypt, wilderness, plenty, forget.

a: I will become a lion for them.
p: Four wild animals. Three of them return in Daniel 7 and Revelation 13.
b: The LORD is a lion (5:14; 13:7, 8), a leopard (13:7), a bear (13:8) and a lioness (13:8). The hunter's pictures appear in the other prophets (Jeremiah 5:6: "and a leopard crouches, watching over their towns"; Lamentations 3:10: "To me he is a lurking bear, a lion in its hiding places."; Amos 5:19). The bear robbed of her cubs is the most dangerous of animals (2 Samuel 17:8; Proverbs 17:12). Three of the four (lion, leopard, bear) are the beasts of Daniel 7:4-6 and the composite beast of Revelation 13:2, which links this chapter to later pictures of empires. In 11:10 the same lion roars to call the children home.
r: Hosea 5:14; Hosea 11:10; Jeremiah 5:6; Lamentations 3:10; Amos 5:19; Daniel 7:4-6; Revelation 13:2

t: 'Watch': the word that sounds like Assyria
p: The verb ashur, 'I will watch', has the same letters as Ashur, 'Assyria'. The Greek reads Assyria.
b: The Hebrew consonants 'shwr are read in the Masoretic Text as a verb, 'ashur, "I will watch" or "lurk". The Greek reads the same letters as a place: "on the road of the Assyrians". The two readings give a pun in either text, and the Plain keeps the verb. The verb shur is used of the LORD's watching in a good sense at 14:8 ("I will watch over him", the same Hebrew word), so the leopard that "watches" the road in 13:7 becomes the one who "watches over" Ephraim in 14:8. The Dead Sea scrolls 4QXIIc and 4QXIIg both have the letters of this word, but the word is restored in the transcriptions, so they cannot be cited. See the variant.

a: tear open the chest that shuts in their heart
p: The Hebrew segor is the 'closing', the chest wall. The Greek has 'the shut-up place of their heart'.
b: Segor is "that which closes", the closure around the heart, here the ribs. The bear tears open the chest to reach the heart. In 2 Samuel 17:8 David's fighters are "like a bear in the open country whose cubs have been taken", angry to the bone. The animals also bring a second picture: after the lion and leopard of 13:7 the bear goes straight to the vital organ and the lioness eats what is inside. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIc (4Q78) reads "like lions of the forest" in the last line where the Masoretic Text has "like a lioness", and the Greek has "young lions of the forest" (skymnoi drymou), so the scroll and the Greek share "of the forest" against the Masoretic Text. The scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves only the start of the verse and agrees with the Masoretic Text. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text; see the variant.

p: The Hebrew shichatka can be a verb ('he has destroyed you') or a noun ('your destruction').
b: The Hebrew shichatkha is a verb in the form "it has destroyed you" or a noun, "your destruction". Other readings: (1) "It has destroyed you, Israel, that you are against me", that is, your rebellion (the Plain's sense); (2) "I have destroyed you, Israel: who is your help?", reading "against me" as "who is in your help", with the Greek: "In your ruin, Israel, who will help you?"; (3) "Your destruction is mine", meaning only the LORD can end it. Either way the last words mean "you are against your own helper". The word "helper" ('ezer) is one Moses uses of the LORD: "He is the shield that helps you" (Deuteronomy 33:29).
orig: שִׁחֶתְךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי־בִי בְּעֶזְרֶךָ (shichatkha Yisra'el ki-vi be'ezrekha)

a: Give me a king and princes
p: Israel's own words when it asked for a king. Hosea quotes them back.
b: The people's request in 1 Samuel 8:5 was: "So now, set up a king for us to judge us, like all the nations." The LORD told Samuel that the elders had rejected him as king (1 Samuel 8:7). Hosea quotes the request and asks what became of it: "Where is that king of yours? Let him save you in all your cities." Hosea's attitude to the monarchy is much debated: (1) anti-monarchic, as in 8:4, 10:3 and 13:10-11, which see the monarchy as itself the people's fault; (2) critical of the northern kings only, because the book looks forward to David (3:5) and the kings of the north were usurpers; (3) a Judean reading that brings in Deuteronomy's law of the king. The LORD also told Samuel to anoint Saul "as ruler over my people Israel", who "will rescue my people" (1 Samuel 9:16), so the Bible is not simply against kingship.
r: 1 Samuel 8:5; 1 Samuel 8:7; 1 Samuel 9:16; Hosea 3:5; Hosea 8:4; Hosea 10:3; Judges 8:22-23

a: Ephraim's guilt is wrapped up in a bundle
p: Guilt is wrapped and kept, to be brought out at the right time.
b: The Hebrew tsarur means "tied up, wrapped" like a coin purse (Genesis 42:35) and tsafunah means "stored, hidden". Job uses the same picture: "You would tie up my rebellion in a pouch with a seal on it," (Job 14:17), and the Song of Moses speaks of the LORD's judgment: "Have I not kept this in store, locked and sealed in my treasure rooms?" (Deuteronomy 32:34). Paul has a related image: "storing up" wrath for the day of wrath (Romans 2:5). The idea is that nothing is forgotten; the guilt is on file. The verse does not say whether the guilt is kept for punishment or for a later forgiveness; the verses around it (13:7-8, 13:11) point to punishment.
orig: צָרוּר עֲוֺן אֶפְרַיִם צְפוּנָה חַטָּאתוֹ (tsarur avon Efrayim tsefunah chatto)

a: he is not a wise son
t: Ephraim as an unborn child who will not come out
p: A baby who stays in the womb at the time of birth dies. The picture is of a nation that refuses to be born.
b: The labor pains are real, but the child (Ephraim) is a "son" without sense, because when the moment comes he does not come out. The danger of a delivery that stalls is shown in Isaiah 37:3: "The children have come right to the mouth of the womb, but there is no strength to push them out." For Hosea the labor is the crisis of the kingdom, and the child's delay is the refusal to repent: the time to turn has come and Ephraim is still inside. The Greek has a different line: "This is your wise son, for he will not endure the breaking of children." Birth language elsewhere in the Bible is also the language of hope (Isaiah 66:7-9; John 16:21).

p: Paul asks 'Where, Death, is your victory?' and 'where is your sting?' Only 'sting' comes from the Greek of Hosea.
b: In 1 Corinthians 15:55 Paul, closing his chapter on the resurrection, writes in Greek: "Where, Death, is your victory? Where, Death, is your sting?" (my rendering from the Greek). The Greek of Hosea 13:14 reads "Where is your penalty (dike), Death? Where is your sting (kentron), Hades?" Paul keeps its two questions and its "sting" in the second, puts "victory" in the place of "penalty" in the first (a link to Isaiah 25:8, which he quotes just before, "Death has been swallowed up in victory"), and addresses Death in both, where the Greek of Hosea addresses Death and then Hades. Many later manuscripts and the King James Version have "Hades" (grave) in his second question and put the sting first, which is closer to Hosea's Greek. The Hebrew words are devareka ("your plagues", from dever) and qotevka ("your destruction"); the Greek renders them "penalty" and "sting". Paul does not name Hosea.
orig: אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת אֱהִי קָטָבְךָ שְׁאוֹל ('ehi devareykha mavet, 'ehi qotevkha she'ol)

t: 'Where', or 'I will be'? The word ehi
p: The Hebrew word ehi can mean 'where' or 'I will be'. The Plain reads 'where'; Jerome's Latin and Luther read 'I will be'.
b: The word 'ehi comes twice in the verse: 'ehi devareykha mavet and 'ehi qotevkha she'ol. It can be read two ways. (1) "Where" (the Plain, and the Greek pou): a spelling of the question word 'ayyeh. The same spelling is at 13:10, where the Greek and the Latin read "where" and the scroll 4QXIIc (4Q78) writes 'ayyeh; that scroll does not preserve 13:14. (2) "I will be" (a short form of 'ehyeh): "I will be your plagues, Death; I will be your destruction, Sheol." This is how Jerome's Latin reads it (ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne, "I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell") and how Luther's German does ("Death, I will be a poison to you"). The same consonants carry both, and the choice changes the sense: "where" mocks Death, whether as a threat to Ephraim or as a victory song, while "I will be" has the LORD himself become Death's undoing.
