The Catholic and Lutheran cards depend on this difference.
orig: אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת אֱהִי קָטָבְךָ שְׁאוֹל ('ehi devareykha mavet, 'ehi qotevkha she'ol)

a: Should I ransom them from the hand of Sheol?
p: The Hebrew allows questions expecting 'no', questions expecting 'yes', or plain statements.
b: The Hebrew has no particle marking the first two lines as questions. Readings: (1) Threat: "Shall I ransom them from Sheol? No! Death, bring your plagues; Sheol, bring your destruction, for pity is hidden from my eyes." Ephraim will die and not be redeemed, and the call to Death and Sheol is an invitation to come (the likeliest reading in the context of 13:12-16, held by many modern commentators). (2) Promise: "I will ransom them from the hand of Sheol; I will redeem them from death. Death, where are your plagues?" The LORD defies Death (the Greek, Jerome's Latin, Luther's German, and the Christian tradition with Paul). (3) A question left open, like the question of 11:8: should I? The Latin and German renderings also depend on reading the Hebrew word 'ehi as "I will be" (see the note on that word). The Plain keeps the questions; the card below lays out how the churches take it. Psalm 49:15 uses the same words as a believer's hope: "God will ransom my life from the hand of Sheol".

a: Pity is hidden from my eyes.
t: The word 'pity' in the last line
p: The Hebrew nocham is the root behind 'comfort', 'relent' and 'pity'. The Greek has 'consolation is hidden'.
b: The noun nocham comes from nacham, "be sorry, relent, comfort". It is found only here, and in Isaiah 57:18 as a related noun. The Plain's "pity" matches the "pity" of 11:8 (nichumim), where the LORD's pity "grows warm". Readings: (1) pity or relenting is hidden, meaning the LORD will not relent (threat); (2) comfort is hidden from the people's eyes. The Greek says paraklesis, "consolation", and the Latin consolatio. Paul leaves this line out. If the first four lines are a promise, this line is awkward; if a threat, it fits perfectly. That is one of the main arguments for the threat reading in the original context. The verb nacham is rendered "change his mind" in the Bible Scroll's fixed terms; the nouns here stay "pity" because "change of mind" does not fit a line about what is hidden from the LORD's eyes, and the note on 11:8 shows the link.

p: The Hebrew yafri, 'he bears fruit', sounds like Ephraim. The phrase 'among brothers' may be 'among reeds'.
b: The verb yafri ("he is fruitful") plays on Efrayim, as in 9:16 ("fruit they will not make") and 14:8. Joseph named his son for being made fruitful (Genesis 41:52), and Jacob blessed Ephraim above Manasseh (Genesis 48:19). The phrase ben 'achim is "a son among brothers", the tribe among the tribes. Some read 'achim as "reeds" (the word in Genesis 41:2 for Egyptian reed-grass) and the line as "he flourishes among reeds", a water-plant that dries up in the east wind. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIc has "brothers" with restored letters. The point is the contrast: the most fruitful of the sons will be struck by a wind from the LORD.

t: The wind that parted the sea
p: The east wind that saved Israel at the sea now attacks Israel.
b: The same hot east wind that rescued Israel at the sea: "All night the LORD made the sea go back by a fierce east wind," (Exodus 14:21), is here "the wind of the LORD" coming up from the wilderness to dry up Ephraim's spring and well. Other prophets use it as the wind of invasion (Ezekiel 17:10; 19:12; Jonah 4:8 for a heat wave). The east wind, warm and dry, comes off the desert and withers crops within a day. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIc reads the text of this line with the Masoretic Text, with some words restored. The wind is a figure for Assyria, but the verse calls it "of the LORD".

p: English 13:16 is the first verse of Hebrew chapter 14. English 14:1-9 are Hebrew 14:2-10.
b: The Hebrew Bible starts its chapter 14 here, so English 13:16 = Hebrew 14:1, and English 14:1-9 = Hebrew 14:2-10. The Greek also starts its chapter 14 here (Greek 14:1 is Samaria and the sword; Greek 14:2 is "Return, Israel"), so a reader of the Greek or the Hebrew will find a verse number one higher than English from 14:1 on. In Jewish synagogue custom the call "Return, Israel" (Hebrew 14:2) names the Sabbath before the Day of Atonement, Shabbat Shuvah, "the Sabbath of Return". The Plain and the notes on this site use the English numbers.

t: War, and the prophet's words about it
p: The picture is of what armies did in the ancient world. The text does not command it.
b: The words are Hosea's picture of what the Assyrian conquest of Samaria will bring. The same acts are recorded in the Bible as the acts of armies: Menahem of Israel, who "cut open all its women who were pregnant" at Tiphsah (2 Kings 15:16); Hazael (2 Kings 8:12); Ammon in Gilead (Amos 1:13). Isaiah 13:16, Nahum 3:10 and Psalm 137:9 have the dashing of infants. These are the fearful terms in which the prophets spoke of invasion; they describe what war did and are presented as the punishment that came, not as an act the LORD commands his people to do. The Plain does not soften them, and the same horror was sometimes done by Israel's own kings, as the passage from 2 Kings shows. See also 10:14.
r: 2 Kings 15:16; 2 Kings 8:12; Amos 1:13; Isaiah 13:16; Nahum 3:10; Psalm 137:9; Hosea 10:14

a: Turn back, Israel, to the LORD your God
t: Shuvah Yisrael: the Sabbath of Return
p: The opening words give the Sabbath before the Day of Atonement its name. English 14:1 is Hebrew 14:2.
b: The Hebrew shuvah Yisra'el, "turn back, Israel", is the first word of the reading from Hosea 14:2-10 (English 14:1-9) that Jewish congregations read, in common custom, on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, called Shabbat Shuvah. The same call is in Jeremiah: "Turn back, Israel, who turned away, the LORD declares." (Jeremiah 3:12). In Hosea it is the key word of the book (6:1; 12:6; 14:1-2, 4) and of the LORD's own turning (11:9, "I will not come back to wreck Ephraim"; 14:4, "my anger has turned away"). The Plain uses "turn back" for repentance and "return" for a physical return. The chapter number shifts: English 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1, so this verse is Hebrew 14:2.

a: you have stumbled over your guilt
p: The Hebrew picture is a person who trips. Rabbinic teaching reads it as comfort.
b: The word kashal, "stumble", is used of falling over an obstacle. Here the obstacle is the people's own guilt. A teaching in the Babylonian Talmud (Yoma 86b) makes a bold use of it: great is repentance, since the verse says "you have stumbled in your guilt", calling a willful sin a stumble, and so through repentance the willful sins are counted as mistakes. That is a rabbinic use, not Hosea's own thought, but the word does frame the book's last lines: "rebels stumble in them" (14:9). In the first case the people stumble over what they did; in the last the rebels stumble on the LORD's straight road.

p: The returning people bring words, not animals.
b: Hosea says that what the people are to bring is devarim, "words", a prayer of confession. This is not a rejection of sacrifice for its own sake (compare 6:6 and 8:13, where the sacrifices please no one because the heart is elsewhere), but the order is clear: the words come first, and they are what turns the people. Other prophets say the same: "A broken spirit: that is the sacrifice for God." (Psalm 51:17); "Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you," (Psalm 141:2). Micah 6:6-8 asks whether the LORD wants thousands of rams, and answers with justice, loyal love and walking humbly. The words are given in the next verses: they are the prayer Hosea puts in the people's mouth, the scripted prayer of repentance.

t: 'Bulls of our lips', 'fruit of lips', and Hebrews 13:15
p: The Hebrew says bulls; the Greek says fruit. Hebrews 13:15 follows the Greek.
b: The Masoretic Text reads parim sefatenu, "bulls, our lips": the bull-offering of the lips, praise paid in place of an animal. The Greek has "fruit of our lips" (karpon cheileon), reading peri, "fruit", for parim. The two Hebrew words differ by one letter (parim and peri), and a mem may have been added or dropped in copying. Hebrews 13:15 follows the Greek: "let us offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name" (my rendering from the Greek). The Latin of Jerome has "the calves of our lips". At Qumran the Community Rule speaks of "the offering of the lips" as the proper sacrifice of the community (1QS 9:4-5), and the rabbis taught that prayer stands in place of the sacrifices (compare Berakhot 26b). See the variant.
r: Hebrews 13:15; Psalm 50:14; Psalm 141:2; Hosea 6:6; Community Rule 9:4-5

a: We will not ride on horses.
t: No help from Assyria, no horses, no idols
p: Three things the people give up: foreign power, military strength, and homemade gods.
b: The three renunciations are the book's three trusts: Assyria (5:13; 7:11; 8:9; 12:1), horses (1:7 promised no help from bow or horse), and the work of their own hands (8:4-6; 13:2). The law of the king told him not to multiply horses or send the people back to Egypt for them (Deuteronomy 17:16). Isaiah's woe is "who lean on horses!" (Isaiah 31:1), and Psalm 20:7 says "These have chariots, and those have horses, but we call on the name of the LORD our God." The Hebrew is "we will not ride on horse", literally: cavalry, the weapon of the empire. The three renunciations are therefore a sign that Israel has quit politics-as-usual in all its forms: foreign allies, arms, and religion by human design.
r: Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 31:1; Psalm 20:7; Hosea 1:7; Hosea 5:13; Hosea 8:4-6

p: The verb is ruham, the root of the name Lo-ruhamah, 'Not Shown Compassion'.
b: The Hebrew yerucham, "is shown compassion", comes from the root that gave the name of Hosea's daughter, Lo-ruhamah, "Not Shown Compassion" (1:6), and the promise that the LORD "will have compassion on Lo-ruhamah" (2:23). The last words of the people's prayer take up the name: in you the one who is "not shown compassion" is shown it. The "child with no father" (yatom) is the orphan whom the Torah protects: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly." (Exodus 22:22) and whom the LORD defends: "God in his holy home is a father to orphans" (Psalm 68:5). In the picture, the exiled northern kingdom has lost its king, its land and its God-given order; it is the orphan, and the prayer rests on the LORD's character.

a: I will heal their turning away.
p: The LORD answers with the same words he used in Jeremiah 3:22.
b: The noun meshuvah, "turning away" (the Plain's term, as in Jeremiah), is the word the book used for Israel's habit of drifting from the LORD (11:7). Jeremiah gives the same line: "Turn back, children who turn away, and I will heal your turning away." (Jeremiah 3:22). Hosea has already shown the LORD as healer: "they did not know that I healed them" (11:3), and the people's own healing hopes (6:1, "he will heal us"), and the false healer in Assyria (5:13). Here the sickness is called by its name, the habit of turning away, and the LORD says he will heal it, not just forgive it. The next line has the same verb, turned: "my anger has turned away from him".
r: Jeremiah 3:22; Hosea 5:13; Hosea 6:1; Hosea 7:1; Hosea 11:3; Hosea 11:7

p: The Hebrew nedavah is the word for a freewill gift.
b: Nedavah is a gift given from willingness and not from duty: the "freewill offering" of Leviticus 22:18 and 23:38, and the "generous rain" of Psalm 68:9. The sentence does not say the LORD will love Israel because of their words in 14:2-3; it says he loves them freely, for his own reasons, and the anger turns by itself. This answers 9:15, where he said, "I will love them no more", and it is the end of the journey that begins in 11:8. The word "love" ('ahav) is the same as in 11:1 and in the first marriage chapters. Hosea does not explain how the LORD can say both. The note on 9:15 sets out the readings.

a: To Israel I will be like the dew.
p: The dew that vanished in 6:4 and 13:3 is now the LORD himself.
b: Dew was the only water in the dry summer, a gift that came unasked, silent, and nightly. In 6:4 the people's loyal love was "dew that rises early and is gone"; in 13:3 the people themselves would be "like the dew that rises early and is gone". Here the LORD says he will be the dew. The reversal is complete: what Israel was not, he will be for Israel. In the Hebrew Bible dew is also a picture of blessing and a king's favor (Proverbs 19:12; Micah 5:7), and the dew of the Hermon (Psalm 133:3) is the dew of blessing. Everything in the next verses grows from the dew: lily, root, branch, olive, grain, vine.

p: The Hebrew has just 'like Lebanon' three times: roots, scent, wine.
b: Lebanon is named three times in the verses 5-7: its roots (14:5), its scent (14:6) and its wine (14:7). The mountain was famous for its cedars, deep-rooted and fragrant (Psalm 92:12; Song of Songs 4:11), and the wine of Helbon (Ezekiel 27:18) was a luxury. The Hebrew of 14:5 is simply "like Lebanon", and the Plain does not add "cedars" or "trees", leaving the image to the reader: a land whose mountains are rooted, scented and fruitful. The lily (shoshannah) is the flower of the Song of Songs (2:1-2), and the roots of Lebanon come in the next line.
r: Psalm 92:12; Song of Songs 2:1; Song of Songs 4:11; Ezekiel 27:18; Hosea 14:6; Hosea 14:7

a: Those who live in his shade will return.
p: The 'he' may be Israel as the tree, or the LORD. The verb is shuv again.
b: The Hebrew is "they will return, those who dwell in his shade". Readings: (1) Israel is the tree (verses 5-6), and its people will live under its shade again; (2) the LORD is the shade (compare Psalm 91:1), and the people will return to live under him. The Greek makes it "under his shelter" and the Latin "under his shade". The verb shuv is the word of the whole chapter (14:1, 2, 4) and of 11:5: the people who refused to turn back (11:5) are now returning. "They will grow grain" and "blossom like the vine" tie the verse to the farming year of 9:2 and 10:1: the grain and wine that failed (9:2) come back. "Fame" (zekher) is also "memorial", the word of 12:5.

a: Ephraim, what more do I have to do with idols?
p: The LORD, Ephraim, or both: the Hebrew can be either. The Greek makes Ephraim the one who is asked.
b: The words "what more do I have to do with idols?" (mah li od la'atsabbim) can be read as the LORD's challenge to Ephraim (he asks what he has to do with idols), or as Ephraim's renunciation in his own voice, answered by the LORD in the next line. The Greek reads "what has he still to do with idols?", with a third-person pronoun, so that the LORD speaks of Ephraim. In each reading the next lines are the LORD's: he answers, watches, and gives fruit. The renunciation of idols echoes 14:3 (the people pledge to stop calling the work of their hands 'Our gods'). The Plain keeps the first-person form and leaves the speaker open.

a: I am like a luxuriant cypress
p: The LORD likens himself to a tree, which is rare. The fruit comes from him, not from Ephraim.
b: The cypress (or juniper, berosh) is an evergreen, thick and unfading. It is the only tree the LORD is compared to in Hosea, an unusual image for a God who elsewhere is the gardener or the vinedresser. The sentence "your fruit comes from me" answers 10:1, where Israel bore fruit "for itself", and 9:16, where Ephraim bore none. It also plays on Ephraim's name, "fruitful", the last time the book does so (9:11-16; 13:15). The Plain's "luxuriant" here translates ra'anan, "leafy, thick"; the vine of 10:1 had a different Hebrew word (boqeq), but the English echo is deliberate. The Greek has "a thick juniper".

a: Who is wise enough to understand these things?
p: The last verse reads like the end of a book of wisdom. Many scholars think a later editor added it.
b: The question echoes the language of Psalm 107:43: "Who is wise? Let him take note of these things, and let them think over the LORD's many acts of loyal love." Many scholars hold that 14:9 is a note added by a later editor, a wisdom teacher, to tell the reader how to read the whole book: Hosea's pictures are hard, but the road is straight. Others say Hosea may have ended his own book this way. The verse also ends the circle begun at 14:1: there the people stumble over their guilt, and here the "rebels" (posh'im, from pesha', "rebellion") stumble in the LORD's ways while the righteous walk. The Talmud uses the verse in a teaching that the same act can be right for one person and a stumble for another (Nazir 23a; Horayot 10b, as reported).
orig: מִי חָכָם וְיָבֵן אֵלֶּה (mi chakham veyaven elleh)
